summary: Extends OSPF link-local signaling to advertise the Local Interface ID, so that a neighbor can learn the Remote Interface ID on the other side of an adjacency.

eli5.summary: Each end of a cable has a number, and this lets one end tell the other what its number is.

questions: what is the ospf local interface id tlv
how does ospf learn the remote interface id
subtitle: A new OSPF Hello and Database Description field that lets neighbors tell each other their interface numbers.

tldr.problem: An OSPF router knows its own Interface ID but must learn the neighbor's (the Remote Interface ID) to tell parallel unnumbered links apart. The older way to learn it, a Link Local TE Opaque LSA, may arrive too late or never.
tldr.mechanism: A new Local Interface ID TLV, type 18, is carried in OSPF link-local signaling (LLS) data in Hello and Database Description packets, so the ID arrives as part of neighbor discovery.
tldr.outcome: Routers can learn the Remote Interface ID before they advertise the link. Implementations that support both mechanisms prefer the LLS value.

facts.label: Carried in
facts.value: OSPF Hello and Database Description packets

today: RFC 8510 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Interface IDs and Why Neighbors Need Them
sections.content:
Every OSPF interface is assigned an Interface ID that uniquely identifies it on the router. RFC 2328 uses it in the Router-LSA Link Data for unnumbered links, taking the value of the MIB-II ifIndex. RFC 4203 calls these the Link Local/Remote Identifiers for GMPLS, and RFC 8379 advertises them in the OSPFv2 Extended Link Opaque LSA.

A router always knows its own (local) ID. The Remote Interface ID, the one on the other side of the adjacency, has to be learned from the neighbor before it can be advertised. This RFC adds a way for the neighbor to tell it, using OSPF link-local signaling from RFC 5613.
sections.eli5: Every plug on a router has a number. Knowing your own plug number is easy. Knowing the number on the other end of the cable means the other router has to tell you.

sections.title: The Problem with Parallel Links
sections.content:
The RFC points to a known OSPFv2 problem in verifying bidirectional connectivity with parallel unnumbered links. If two parallel unnumbered links join a pair of routers and each is advertised from only one direction, another router could treat these two one-way links as one valid bidirectional link. If every link is advertised with both its Local and Remote Interface IDs, the advertisements from both sides can be cross-checked.

The existing way to learn the remote ID, from RFC 4203, uses the Link Local TE Opaque LSA. It has two drawbacks the RFC names. LSAs can only flow over an adjacency in Exchange state or greater, and each side progresses independently, so a link may be advertised before the LSA arrives and then advertised again, with no guarantee the neighbor ever sends it. And that LSA was defined for MPLS Traffic Engineering, although the remote ID is useful where MPLS TE is not used.
sections.eli5: If two routers are joined by two identical-looking cables, you need each cable's number from both ends to be sure which is which. The old way of asking could be slow, or never answered.

sections.title: The Local Interface ID TLV
sections.content:
To make the exchange part of neighbor discovery, the RFC extends OSPF link-local signaling to carry the Local Interface ID in OSPF Hello and Database Description (DD) packets. The new Local Interface ID TLV is an LLS TLV with three fields: Type (18), Length (4 octets) and Local Interface ID, the sender's own value.

The signaling is applicable to all OSPF interface types other than virtual links.
sections.eli5: It is a small labeled slip tucked into the hello message. The label says what the slip is, how long it is, and then it holds the number.

sections.title: Working Alongside RFC 4203
sections.content:
If an implementation supports both the new LLS signaling and the Link Local TE Opaque LSA, it MUST prefer the value received through LLS when both come from the same router. An implementation that signals through the LSA MAY keep doing so for backward compatibility. If it also supports the LLS mechanism, it MUST signal the same Local Interface ID through both.

When the ID changes, which the RFC calls rare, the two values may briefly differ. This is temporary, and they should match once the next Hello or Link Local TE Opaque LSA is regenerated by the originator.
sections.eli5: If a router gets the number two ways and they disagree, it trusts the hello. The two ways are supposed to say the same thing, and quickly catch up if the number changes.

sections.title: The IANA Code Point
sections.content: IANA has allocated value 18, the Local Interface ID TLV, in the "Link Local Signalling TLV Identifiers (LLS Types)" subregistry of the OSPF Link Local Signalling (LLS) Type/Length/Value Identifiers registry.
sections.eli5: The official list of allowed slip labels now has number 18 reserved for this one.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The security considerations of OSPF link-local signaling (RFC 5613) also apply here. The advertised ID is used to tell parallel links apart, so tampering with the TLV could cause a wrong neighbor Interface ID to be advertised in the OSPFv2 Extended Link Opaque LSA and could prevent the link from being used. If authentication is used in the OSPF routing domain, the Cryptographic Authentication TLV SHOULD also be used to protect the LLS block.

Receiving a malformed Local Interface ID TLV MUST NOT cause a hard router or OSPF process failure. Malformed LLS TLVs or sub-TLVs SHOULD be logged, but the logging MUST be rate-limited to prevent denial-of-service attacks. The RFC sees no privacy concern, since the ID is a locally unique identifier not expected to carry information about the device owner or traffic.
sections.eli5: Someone sneaking in a wrong number could make a link unusable, so the hello should be protected. A garbled slip must never crash the router.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the value, in octets.

fields.name: Local Interface ID
fields.desc: The sender's own Interface ID for this link.
